title: Cheerfully Sinister: Inside Trevor Winkfield’s Puzzling, Playful Canvases
summary: A young man in a fish-topped helmet holds a pot beneath a lightbulb that dispenses snowflake-marked tokens. Outside the window, those same tokens drift across a pink and blue mountain. This is “The Student” (1999), one of eight acrylic-on-linen works in Trevor Winkfield’s exhibition “The Mermaid’s Revenge” at Tibor de Nagy gallery in Manhattan. Painted between 1991 and 2001, these large-scale pieces — some stretching over five feet wide — are meticulously detailed, flatly colored, and cheerfully incomprehensible. Winkfield, now in his 80s, has carved an idiosyncratic path since moving from England to New York in 1969. He ran a poetry magazine, collaborated with New York School poets like John Ashbery, and translated the eccentric French writer Raymond Roussel, known for novels built on homophonic wordplay. Critics have long tried to link Winkfield’s collage-like paintings to Roussel’s linguistic puzzles, but the artist insists there is no key. “As literary as Winkfield is, he is equally a visual person. This complete duality is what makes him inimitable,” notes the gallery. The paintings depict solitary figures — a navigator, an astrologer, a self-portrait — engaged in obscure tasks. Their bodies are assembled from discrete, flat shapes, like intricate shadow puppets, with occasional volumetric details that disrupt the airless surface. Colors are saturated and playful, yet a subtle unease lingers: the world is “simultaneously brightly colored, slightly sinister, and cheerfully incomprehensible.” Winkfield paints on a table, and these works come from a decade when he had access to a larger studio, allowing him to scale up his visions. The exhibition, on view through July 31, is a testament to the power of imagination over literal meaning. In an art world often obsessed with transparent social messages, Winkfield’s hermetic scenes offer a liberating alternative. His rejection of certainty reminds us that art can be a space for pure invention — a place where a fish helmet and floating tokens make perfect, mysterious sense.
why_it_matters: Winkfield's work challenges the expectation that art must deliver a clear social message; it reminds young viewers that art can be a space for imagination, mystery, and personal interpretation, which fosters creative thinking and tolerance for ambiguity.

background_read: Trevor Winkfield, born in England in the 1940s, is a painter and poet who became part of the New York avant-garde after moving to the city in 1969.
The Tibor de Nagy Gallery, established in 1950, is a pioneering New York gallery known for its close ties to the New York School of poets and painters, including John Ashbery and Frank O'Hara.

John Ashbery (1927–2017) was one of America's most celebrated poets, winning the Pulitzer Prize for his collection 'Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror'; his playful, elusive style resonates with Winkfield's visual puzzles.
Raymond Roussel (1877–1933) was a wealthy French writer whose unusual novels, built on elaborate linguistic games and absurd plots, influenced Surrealists and experimental artists.

The New York School was an informal group of 1950s-60s poets and artists (including Ashbery, O'Hara, and painters like Willem de Kooning) who collaborated and shared a spirit of spontaneity and abstraction.

perspectives.description: Fans celebrate Winkfield's commitment to pure imagination, seeing his paintings as joyful escapes from the noise of everyday life, where the viewer's own creativity completes the meaning.
Skeptics may dismiss the work as self-indulgent or meaningless—mere decoration that refuses to engage with real-world issues, which can feel irrelevant in times of crisis.

Historically, art that resists easy interpretation (from Dada to Abstract Expressionism) has often pushed boundaries and expanded what art can be; Winkfield fits into this tradition of valuing process and ambiguity over message.
As AI-generated art and algorithm-driven content rise, Winkfield's hand-painted, deliberately obscure scenes may become even more valued as expressions of individual, unexplainable human creativity.
